431.history: The southern Seann Skell was a fishing harbour with salt-sheds and the house of Brìde's Rite when the company of shipmasters, Comann nan Sciobairean, leased the sheds in {{year:VI-0008}} and built there the first works for the making of dubhan outside the north. Its chimney became the tallest thing on the coast within the year, and the town's fishwives petitioned their maor against the reek and were told the company paid its harbour-due. The works sold their first year's making to the south-coast boats and the lamp-houses of Cathair dhearg; Peigi nic Ascaill came down from Comhairle nan Taighean-solais to see them, fitted her baffle to every furnace in the row, and at length took service there as master-fitter. In the long shed of the works Comann nan Goibhnean-ceangail were chartered in {{year:VI-0045}}, twelve masters sworn under a banner of a black swan on grey, and Riaghailt na Cairte let go the Tuathaich hands who had turned the lights. The last coal flame of the coast was carried here in a closed lantern and let burn out on Brìde's altar. In the war An dàrna cabhlach and then An naoidheamh rèisimeid were raised at the town, the second of that name in the regimental list, told apart by the clerks as the Seann Skell of the coast. In the present year the altar-coal of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail is drawn here by lot among the houses, in Brìde's yard, from four baskets carried south from Achadh dhomhain.
431.known_for: the shipmasters' dubhan works, Comann nan Goibhnean-ceangail' charter and the lot of the altar-coal

151.history: The fair town on Rathad na Fèille below the capital kept its great fair and its fair court through the age, but lost its coal. In the third year of Linn an Dubhain the last carter of coal on Rathad na Fèille sold his cart and kept his horse, and the justice of Cùirt na Fèille, Fionnlagh mac Gille-Chaluim, scraped the painted coal ceiling off the board by the toll-house door, since no seller kept it. His clerk Ùna nic Ailein entered the striking in the court's day-book, which she kept until the book closed with no entry in the year of the column. In the war An t-Ionmhas set a clerk at the town's dubhan pump to take the tithe, one part in twelve of every sale, and the young Cailean Ros sat in the coldest corner of the toll-house's upper room to do it. In {{year:VI-0113}} the fair-ground was cleared for the regiments, the stall-holders numbering their timbers to set them up again, and the first and third regiments camped on it before they went down Rathad na Fèille to Muileann ghlas. The fair came back to its ground in the autumn after the war, and in the present year it draws traders from every shire the state holds, the Tuathaich wool sold on its northern day through Dia-thìrich factors, as it has been for a generation.
151.known_for: Cùirt na Fèille's scraped board, and the fair-ground given to the regiments

246.history: The town of the great library lay up its valley road through the age with the paper-mill's race below it and Leabharlann Muileann chaol above. The carriers of the library road brought up the first word of the northern fuel, and the black cake was burned at its market before the chronicler had seen it. In the dry first year the mill-race ran too low to turn the paper-mill's wheel, and the keeper Raghnall mac Mhuirich ordered no fire in the reading-room before the middle of an t-Samhain and none after dark, a rule the house kept in every hard winter after. Sìleas nic Rath came up the valley in the eleventh year as clerk to Seanchaidh na Rìoghachd, and began here the box of slips in which the fuel's name was spelled four ways; Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh re-headed fourteen years of Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd in the house by lamplight when the new count of the years was proclaimed, and set Comann nan Gualadairean' dies beside their oath-stone in the lower gallery. The town saw its first soldiery when An dàrna rèisimeid was raised at Àth dhìreach to guard the library road, and a sergeant of that regiment kept the gate in the present year. In the new wing's lower gallery stands the room sealed in {{year:VI-0128}}, behind a door of oak two inches thick; its key hangs on a cord under the keeper's shirt.
246.known_for: the library, its re-headed chronicle, and the sealed room

95.history: The chief harbour of the Tuathaich was the first town of the Dia-thìrich kingdom to see the northern fuel sold, a black cake at its market in the first year, and the first to be asked about it: Comhairle nam Mèinnean's two surveyors lodged four days at Harker's inn on the harbour, were answered civilly everywhere in good Dia-thìris, and were told nothing. Tional nan Tuathach sat at Caol mhòr through the whole age. Martha Greaves took its chair after Daniel Frayne's death; the rebound minute-books were laid in its press, the key on the speaker's ring. The fitters of Caol mhòr turned the light at Baile chrom, and when Riaghailt na Cairte let them go from the southern works they came home and fitted engines without a guild, so that within a few years the harbour held more dubhan boats than any port of its size in the south. The five western pit towns walked out of Tional nan Tuathach here in {{year:VI-0055}}, and their benches were kept chalked in the roll with nothing after them. In the war An ceathramh cabhlach searched the harbour's boats and Tional nan Tuathach's granaries were opened to the families of the western hills, whose names Thomas Rook entered in a register that ran past three hundred. In the present year Peter Hale keeps the chair and opens Tional nan Tuathach's book in his own hand.
95.known_for: Tional nan Tuathach, the fitters' boats, and the register of the western families
